sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, BDPI: Uro
sources.note: Introduction and history distinguish the living Peruvian Uro people, Lake Titicaca presence, Inca-era tribute synthesis, later records, language loss, family islands, tourism, totora knowledge, and continuity.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, Ficha Uro
sources.note: Pages 1 to 5 summarize official identity, history, languages, family islands, fishing, tourism, totora engineering, and source limitations.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, Resolución Viceministerial 005-2013-VMPCIC-MC
sources.note: Pages 2 to 5 describe qilli blocks, reed layers, maintenance, houses, boats, tools, drying, sails, and the official heritage declaration.

sources.title: Congress of Peru, Law 30729
sources.note: Single-page 2018 law declares protection of the Uros and Uros Chulluni, especially cultural and language recovery, to be of national interest and public necessity.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, State recognition of the Uros
sources.note: 9 March 2018 recognition, community authorities, Qhas Qut Suñis self-presentation, cultural and language recovery, and modern wastewater planning.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, Uro language revitalization course
sources.note: 1 December 2025 report: 88 pupils, 12 teachers, two course stages, basic vocabulary, conversation, poetry and songs, with an intermediate and adult course planned.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, National Registry of Indigenous Languages, Andean Languages
sources.note: PDF pages 343 to 345 distinguish Uru-Chipaya varieties, report about three hundred Ch’imu words collected at Puno in 1929, classify Peruvian Uro as extinct, and record language-recovery work.

sources.title: DOBES Uru-Chipaya documentation, People and Culture
sources.note: Separates Chipaya and Ayparavi, Lake Poopó, Irohito, and Puno floating-island communities; documents fishing, bird hunting, children’s meetings, language shift, tourism study, and modern livelihoods.

sources.title: DOBES Uru-Chipaya documentation, Language
sources.note: Defines documented varieties, late nineteenth-century documentation, Ch’imu material, current Chipaya vitality, structural cautions, and Aymara influence.

sources.title: DOBES Uru-Chipaya documentation, Project
sources.note: Describes community recordings, native-speaker interviewing, alphabet teaching, water interviews, Irohito recordings, Lake Poopó instruments, and limits of project coverage.

sources.title: Katja Hannß, Vocabulario Uru (Uchumataqu)
sources.note: 2013 historical vocabulary preserves source-specific transcriptions; the water entry includes Lehmann’s 1929 Ch’imu form hŭắsē and multiple distinct Uru forms.

sources.title: Katja Hannß, Vocabulario Uru: introduction and transcription key
sources.note: Pages i to iv explain the Irohito or Ancoaqui focus, 1894 to 2005 source range, semantic organization, and intentionally unstandardized historical transcriptions.

sources.title: Instituto Riva-Agüero PUCP, El Uro de la Bahía de Puno
sources.note: Publisher record identifies Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino’s 2016 study, the Titicaca-Coipasa aquatic axis, fishing communities, and Chipaya as the surviving related language.

sources.title: PUCP, El Uro de la bahía de Puno: interview with Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino
sources.note: 27 June 2017 interview explains Lehmann’s 1929 material, language replacement, multilingual history, the Peruvian language’s extinction, and parent-to-child Chipaya transmission.

sources.title: Catherine J. Julien, The Uru Tribute Category
sources.note: Pages 55 to 76 analyze 1567 and 1570s administrative records, lower tribute rates, category meanings, language distribution, occupational stereotypes, and why colonial labels are not simple ethnic maps.

sources.title: Garci Diez de San Miguel, Visita hecha a la provincia de Chucuito en 1567
sources.note: Primary colonial survey and 1964 paleographic edition; preliminary note and folios record questions, testimony, tribute, and socioeconomic evidence after conquest, with administrative bias.

sources.title: Nathan Wachtel, Men of the water: the Uru problem
sources.note: Chapter summary maps a sixteenth-century aquatic axis, estimates a large Uru population, and identifies dehumanizing stereotypes in colonial and later scholarship.

sources.title: Nathan Wachtel, Hommes d’eau: le problème uru
sources.note: Open 1978 article, especially pages 1127 to 1159, examines the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century aquatic axis, social categories, language, tribute, mobility, and hostile stereotypes.

sources.title: Barbieri and colleagues, The Genetic History of Indigenous Populations of the Peruvian and Bolivian Altiplano
sources.note: PLOS ONE 8(9):e73006, Introduction and Materials and Methods, Population Samples and DNA Extraction: Uro meanings, distinct sampled communities, multilingual histories, and informed consent.

sources.title: Michael Kent, A importância de ser uro
sources.note: Peer-reviewed 2011 ethnography covers Uro self-representation, disputed identity, territorial politics, genomics, oral histories, and the danger of making DNA an identity test.

sources.title: Michael Kent, Práticas territoriais indígenas entre a flexibilidade e a fixação
sources.note: Mana 17(3), pages 549 to 582: island merging and splitting, household and community flexibility, neighboring relations, state mapping, and conflicts produced by fixing boundaries.

sources.title: Julio Villca, Rita Suaña, and collaborators, Saberes y conocimientos de los uros de Puno
sources.note: Community research, printed pages 85 to 105: territory, islands, boats, teaching, group fishing, seasonal eggs, family foods, reported remedies, health posts, and explicit 2019 testimonies.

sources.title: Gina Hallasi Puntaca, Water quality on the Uros floating islands
sources.note: 2018 UNAP thesis record and abstract describe May to July 2016 sampling at five named islands for microbial, physical, and chemical drinking-water measures.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, COVID-19 vaccination reaches the Uro people
sources.note: 8 July 2021 report documents Uro island vaccination, health-network coordination, community authorities, and information and materials in Aymara and Quechua; explicit Aymara interpretation concerns other Puno communities.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Housing, Resolución Directoral 079-2022-VIVIENDA-DGAA
sources.note: Section 3.2 describes a current Cappi Los Uros project for 256 residents and 109 students: water treatment and twenty floating composting-sanitation modules.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Culture, BDPI locality: Uros Chulluni
sources.note: Community record gives 1975 recognition, 1994 title, 2007 population and age data, Indigenous-language figures, and six initial, primary, and secondary education institutions.

sources.title: Archivo General de la Nación, Uros-Chulluni recognition record
sources.note: 19 July 2025 report identifies the 23 October 1975 recognition resolution, community request, leaders, and more than one hundred currently inhabited floating islands.

sources.title: EMSAPUNO, Memoria Anual 2024
sources.note: Annual report project CUI 2574386 records Uros Chulluni potable-water construction, dates, financing, 91.05 percent physical progress, and stated access objective.

sources.title: Municipality of Puno, Potable water for Uros Chulluni
sources.note: 1 April 2024 report documents co-financing and participation by municipal, utility, and Uros Chulluni authorities in the water project.

sources.title: OEFA, Water-quality monitoring near the Uros islands
sources.note: 2025 field report records joint OEFA, binational-lake, and water-authority monitoring with Uros Chulluni municipal and community leaders.

sources.title: Amanda Aland, Fishing Economies and Ethnic Specialization under Inca Rule
sources.note: Oxford Handbook chapter abstract frames Titicaca fishing under Inca rule through archaeological and ethnohistorical evidence, occupational specialization, administration, and tribute.

sources.title: Capriles, Moore, Domic, and Hastorf, Fishing and environmental change in the Lake Titicaca Basin
sources.note: Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 34:66–77 analyzes faunal remains from 367 flotation samples at five sites dated 1500 BCE to 1100 CE and finds fishing intensity varied through time.

sources.title: Dominique Levieil and Benjamin Orlove, Local Control of Aquatic Resources
sources.note: American Anthropologist 92(2):362–382 reports contemporary communal fishing territories and ecological variation around Lake Titicaca; modern evidence, not a 1492 cadastral map.

sources.title: Bolivia IPELC, Review of Uru-Chipaya language materials
sources.note: 2 May 2024 report names a standardized Spanish–Uru-Chipaya dictionary, teaching booklet, and other educational texts under review by the Uru language and culture institute.
